sweep_summary: Navajo (nava1243, catalog tonal on Sapir & Hoijer 1967 via SPA 1979). Four works with stress in the title reduce to two works. (1) Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' (Glottolog 167470) was located through the ANLA JSON API (record CA965L1976b) and downloaded as an 86-page scan-only scan (draft + typescript) from uafanlc.alaska.edu; three typescript pages were scanned at 300 dpi and the rest read from contact sheets. It is a comparative tonogenesis paper: PA vowel constriction and final glottalization become tone in the daughters, with Navajo showing constricted > low tone, non-constricted > high tone (pp.9, 11, 14). It never mentions stress or accent placement in Navajo: silent on the catalog's classification, priority none. (2) McDonough 2003 'The prosody of interrogative and focus constructions in Navajo' appears three times in Glottolog (181704, 665186 dated 2002, and 673539 mis-authored to the editors Carnie et al.); all are the same Benjamins chapter, whose open author preprint was already held by the project. It is an intonation/focus study, but states first-hand that Navajo has a tone on every syllable, no metrical structure, and only default rightmost (verb-stem) phonetic prominence: confirms tonal. No item contradicts or refines the catalog; no new deciding source found; nothing left to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title.alaska.edu host has a certificate-chain problem; automated download -k was needed).

new_statements.quote: "McDonough (1990, 1996, 2000a, 2000b) has argued that metrically based structure has no presence in Navajo, and phenomena explained as metrical in Northern Athabaskan are the result of exclusively morphological imperatives in Navajo." ... "Instrumental studies indicate that the verb stem has many of the properties commonly associated to prominence: longer durations, pitch range expansion, semantic salience (McDonough and Ladefoged 1993, McDonough 1999). ... The stem is the only place in the word where the full set of phonemic contrasts occurs."
new_statements.citation: McDonough, Joyce. 2003. The prosody of interrogative and focus constructions in Navajo. In A. Carnie, H. Harley & M. Willie (eds.), Formal Approaches to Function in Grammar (Linguistik Aktuell 62), 191-206. Amsterdam: Benjamins. Author preprint, UR Research repository.
new_statements.locator: preprint p.3 (sec. 1.2, the text) and p.17 (sec. 3.3, the text)
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the leading instrumental phonetician of Navajo: the language has a tone specified on every syllable and no metrical (stress) structure; the only word-level prominence is the phonetic salience of the word-final verb stem, which is a morphological, not a stress, effect. This agrees with the catalog's tonal coding built on Sapir & Hoijer 1967 ('evenly stressed syllables, each bearing a tone'). This file was already held and cited as supporting evidence in the catalog record (downloaded 2026-09-16); nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title is stronger. Leer 1976, the only genuinely new item, is a comparative tonogenesis paper and is silent on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Kiser, Michele. 2014. Analyzing Navajo Discourse: Investigating Form and Function of Intonational Units in Referential Discourse. PhD dissertation (Linguistics), University of New Mexico. UNM Digital Repository, Linguistics ETDs 22.
tone_statements.quote: Navajo utilizes linguistic tone. In linguistic terms, tone is the alternation in pitch in a language that distinguishes words either lexically or grammatically. Navajo is a tonal language; syllables are inherently low tone by default, and marked syllables have high tones ... Most often in Navajo tone is used to inflect and distinguish words that would otherwise be homonyms. As seen below in example (14) the difference between second and third person singular is realized as the high tone /í/ ... (14) a. dílkos ... ‘you are coughing’ b. dilkos ... ‘he/she/it is coughing’
tone_statements.locator: pp. 21-22, section 1.7.1 'Intonation and Linguistic Tone in Navajo'; restated p. 64, section 3.4.3
tone_statements.summary: Discourse/intonation-unit study; tone treated briefly as background: two-way contrast, syllables low by default vs marked high, lexical and grammatical function, minimal pairs (dílkos/dilkos, doo/dóó, 'azee'/'azéé'). Nothing on downstep or TBU.

tone_statements.quote: Navajo vowels have low or high tone. A high tone vowel is indicated by an accent mark over the vowel. The short and the long vowels may be high toned as in the following examples: [...] Long vowels, written as two vowels can also have a rising or falling tone. When a low long vowel is followed by a particle that has a high tone, the second vowel becomes high, resulting in a rising tone; and when a high long vowel is followed by a particle with low tone, then the second vowel becomes low, resulting in a falling tone
tone_statements.locator: p. 5, sec. 1.1 'The Vowels', subsection 'Tone'; summary sentence also on p. 4: 'Navajo vowels show a contrast for length and nasality and high and low tone, with rising and falling tones only on long vowels.'

tone_statements.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 2005. Athabaskan Tone (1979). In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269), 55-136. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/cilt.269.07kra.
tone_statements.quote: The S-K-N basic pattern with low tone from constriction or glottalization and high tone in its absence Leer has called “low-marked”. ... Navajo, like Sarcee, is well known as a low-marked tone language. The only exception to over 60 examples with full vowels is high-toned ... “fog”, already discussed. ... For reduced stems in Navajo, the rule is simply that all of them have low tone, a notable characteristic of Apachean historical phonology, and the ultimate extension of the Sarcee lowering of the tone in non-constricted reduced stem-vowels.
tone_statements.locator: typescript p. 11, sec. 3 (definition of low-marked) and pp. 57-58, sec. 6.4 'Comments on Each Language in Table'
tone_statements.summary: Navajo (standing for Apachean) classed as a low-marked tone language: full stem vowels low where PA had constriction, high otherwise; all reduced stem vowels low. Noun stems only; nothing on TBU, downstep or stress. 10+ marked forms.

tone_statements.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1999. Tonogenesis in Athabaskan. In Shigeki Kaji (ed.), Proceedings of the Symposium Cross-Linguistic Studies of Tonal Phenomena: Tonogenesis, Typology, and Related Topics (Tokyo, Dec. 10-12, 1998), 37-66. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
tone_statements.quote: In the low-marked tone languages, PA constriction appears as low tone, opposed to unmarked (non-low) tone. ... The Southern Athabaskan languages (Navajo and Apache) ... constitute a low-marked branch of Athabaskan. ... In Southern Athabaskan (Navajo and Apache), we find the same sort of innovation in the tonal system, with one further development: mid tone merged with low tone on short vowels. 27. Tonal development in Southern Athabaskan: a. PA *V· → Southern Athabaskan *v́· b. PA *V̓· → Southern Athabaskan *v̀· c. PA *v, *v̌ → Southern Athabaskan *v̀
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Navajo classed as a low-marked Athabaskan tone language: PA constricted vowels > low tone vs unmarked high; long full vowels high, short vowels low after a mid/low merger. Count 2 inferred from the stated low vs non-low opposition, not an explicit Navajo count. Nothing on TBU, downstep or stress.

tone_statements.quote: Also, vowels may be either high tone or low tone; the difference in tone of the vowel is the sole distinguishing factor phonetically between many pairs of morphemes. Still, we will see that there is much to be said in favor of an analysis that derives all high tone vowels from low tone vowels upon "absorption" of a following consonant. ... All four vowel qualities exhibit the same eight variants for nasality, length, and tone, though for lack of space we have indicated this only for the vowel [i] in Table III.

tone_statements.summary: Two tones, high vs low, coded as a binary feature [high tone] on every vowel (Table III; long vowels count as one segment). Author proposes deriving all high tones from low tone plus 'absorption' of a following consonant; p.18: Hoijer treats high and low tone as phonemes on every syllabic.

(2) The classification tonal (H/L lexical tone on every syllable; word stress explicitly denied as 'evenly stressed syllables'; stem-final phonetic prominence hedged as stress-like) rests on the 1967 reference grammar plus McDonough's phonetic work. The best modern source, McDonough 2003 The Navajo Sound System, is not yet obtained, but McDonough's open 2003 Benjamins preprint downloaded now states outright that 'metrically based structure has no presence in Navajo', that Navajo is 'a tone language with a tone specified for each syllable (Sapir-Hoijer 1967, Young and Morgan 1987)

McDonough (1990, 1996, 2000a, 2000b) has argued that metrically based structure has no presence in Navajo, and phenomena explained as metrical in Northern Athabaskan are the result of exclusively morphological imperatives in Navajo." p.4: "Navajo has been classified as a tone language with a tone specified for each syllable (Sapir-Hoijer 1967, Young and Morgan 1987)." p.17: "Instrumental studies indicate that the verb stem has many of the properties commonly associated to prominence: longer durations, pitch range expansion, semantic salience"

sources.note: Instrumental study of yes/no-question and focus intonation; finds no tonal intonation and no focus accent. On word level it states that Navajo has a tone on every syllable, no metrical structure, and that any 'accent' can only fall by default on the rightmost content morpheme, the verb stem, which is phonetically prominent (longer, pitch-range expansion). No word-stress rule; consistent with the catalog's tonal coding.

sources.note: Nothing on Navajo word stress. The only usable prosodic content is the standard Navajo high-tone morphophonology (ni-absorption after Kari 1976), which is compatible with, but adds nothing to, the catalog's tonal coding (Sapir & Hoijer 1967; McDonough 2003: tone on every syllable, no metrical structure). The lone 'stress' sentence concerns Hungarian (Kiss 1985) and is not about this language.

sources.note: This work describes Hare (Athapaskan; Glottolog hare1244, a dialect of North Slavey nort2942). Navajo appears only as comparative cognate data (Sapir's field notes, forms carry acute/grave tone marks) and in two remarks on verb-stem allomorphy and heavy/light stem finals. No sentence states the Navajo stress or tone system. Nothing here bears on the nava1243 coding (tonal, lexical-tone).

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1976. Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76, 24 pp. handwritten + 30 pp. typescript. Alaska Native Language Archive item CA965L1976b. [Glottolog id 167470, listed by Glottolog as a comparative study]
sources.quote: p.9: "In PA there were two suprasegmentals, which in stems were restricted to closed syllables, and could co-occur. They are vowel nasalization (V̨) and what I call vowel constriction (V̓). Vowel constriction is manifest in modern Athabaskan languages as tone." p.11: "In Kutchin, Tanana, Upper Kuskokwim, Sarcee and Navajo as well as other languages not included in this study, the reflex of V̊ [non-constricted] is high tone and the reflex of V̓ [constricted] is low tone. ... In Navajo both *CV̓C, *CvC > CvC; the reflexes of V and V̓ do not contrast in stems having reduced vowels."
sources.locator: typescript p.9 (PDF page 13) and p.11 (PDF page 15); also p.14 (PDF page 18); scanned samples in leer1976_ocr_samples/
sources.note: A comparative-historical paper on how Proto-Athabaskan vowel constriction and stem-final glottalization became tone in the daughter languages; Navajo is one of thirteen languages whose stem-tone reflexes are tabulated (constricted vowel > low tone, non-constricted > high tone; final glottal stop > low tone, p.14). It says nothing about word stress or accent placement in Navajo. Scanned image PDF (86 pp. = annotated draft + clean typescript), no text; three typescript pages scanned at 300 dpi, remainder read from contact sheets.

The nasal cannot assume the coda position (in any prefixal structure) and must be an onset, and this must be supported by epenthesis. The high tone is realized on the epenthetic vowel.
